title: Thanksgiving owed that venials are not imputed unto death
source_text: XV. Tertium autem ejus corollarium sic habet: Obligamur Deo ad gratificationem, & gratiarum actionem, ex hoc quod peccata nostra venialia non imputat ad mortem, sicut tenemur ex remissione mortalium; quoniam utrobique concurrit misericordia Dei, non imputans peccata, nisi ad poenam temporalem, quae de sua indignitate imputabilia sunt ad mortem, unum de possibili, aliud de lege statuta. Imo forsan ita diceretur de omnibus justitiis nostris; quae quantum de se sunt, sunt sicut pannus menstruatae; praesertim post peccatum, aut absente gratia.
pass_a_gloss: But his third corollary runs thus: We are bound to God for gratitude and thanksgiving from this, that He does not impute our venial sins unto death, just as we are bound from the remission of mortals; because in both places the mercy of God concurs, not imputing sins except unto temporal punishment, which from their own unworthiness are imputable unto death—one as possible, the other by statute law. Nay, perhaps the same would be said of all our righteousnesses, which as far as they are of themselves are as a menstruous cloth, especially after sin, or when grace is absent.
pass_b_english: Even venials, for Gerson, deserve thanks that God does not impute them unto death—as with remitted mortals.
He extends the same mercy-logic toward our righteousnesses as filthy rags apart from grace.

choices.why: Isaianic image for righteousness apart from grace.
